t: Longest Nice Substring - Case-Pairing Bitmasks and Divide & Conquer
o: A window is nice exactly when its lowercase letters and its uppercase letters coincide as sets - every letter present must appear in both cases. Example 1, `"YazaAay"`: 'z' has no 'Z', so no nice window covers index 2; inside "Ya" nothing pairs, while "aAay" splits again at the unpartnered trailing 'y', leaving "aAa" (length 3) as the answer. Example 2, `"Bb"`, is entirely nice. Example 3, `"c"`, admits nothing, hence the empty string. Two facts drive the solutions: with n <= 100 even testing all windows passes easily, and any letter lacking its case-partner somewhere in the string can never sit inside a nice substring, which licenses splitting the problem at such letters.
k: Track presence with two 26-bit masks (lowercase seen, uppercase seen); a window is nice iff the masks are equal.
A character whose opposite case is absent from the whole string cannot belong to any nice substring - a natural split point.
Recursion depth is bounded by the alphabet: each divide-and-conquer level removes at least one letter pair.

a.n: Approach 1: All Windows with Incremental Bitmasks
a.i: Fix the left end, sweep the right end, and fold each new character into a lowercase mask and an uppercase mask. Masks update in O(1), so each of the O(n^2) windows is judged instantly: nice iff lower == upper. Updating the answer only on strictly greater length preserves the earliest-occurrence tie-break automatically.
s: For each start i, reset both masks to 0.
Extend j to the right, setting the bit for s[j]'s letter in the matching mask.
When the masks are equal, window s[i..j] is nice - keep it if strictly longer than the best.
Return the best window (empty if none qualified).
a.t: O(n^2) time - each window extension is O(1) thanks to incremental mask updates.
a.sp: O(1) auxiliary space beyond the returned substring.

a.n: Approach 2: Divide and Conquer on Bad Characters
a.i: If some character of the current string has no case-partner anywhere in it, no nice substring can include that position, so the answer lives wholly to its left or wholly to its right - recurse on both pieces and keep the longer (preferring the left on ties keeps the earliest occurrence). If every character is paired, the whole string is nice. Each recursion discards at least one letter pair from future consideration, bounding depth by 26 and yielding near-linear behavior in practice.
s: Base case: length below 2 returns the empty string.
Collect the string's character set; locate the first character whose swapcase is missing from the set.
If none exists, the entire string is nice - return it.
Otherwise recurse on the segments left and right of that character and return the longer result (left wins ties).
a.t: About O(26 * n) - every call scans its segment once and depth is capped by 26 removable letter pairs.
a.sp: O(26 * n) worst case for substring slices and the recursion stack.

w: Given n <= 100, the bitmask brute force is a perfectly respectable interview answer - state that, then offer divide and conquer as the elegant upgrade. Mind the tie-break: strict '>' when updating in Approach 1, left preference ('>=') when merging in Approach 2. Be ready to explain why sliding window does not apply: adding a letter can break niceness while removing a different one restores it, so the predicate is not monotone in window growth. Follow-ups: scale to n = 10^5 (divide and conquer survives, brute force does not), or generalize 'nice' to digits/paired symbols.
